issues.legal_issue: An unregistered writing may be relied on to establish severance of joint status, but not to prove a formal partition by metes and bounds where it requires registration.
material_facts: A suit sought partition of properties claimed to belong to a joint family.
The defendants relied on an unregistered writing relating to an earlier partition.

The lower courts found a prior partition and separate enjoyment of the properties, supported by evidence of separate possession, cultivation, tax payments, division of a house, separate dealings in properties, separate accounts of acquisition compensation, and separate property records.
The first appellate court relied on the writing to establish severance of joint status, rather than treating it as an admissible deed proving allotments by metes and bounds.
issues.conclusion: The unregistered writing could be relied on to establish severance of joint status, although it could not serve as a registered deed proving a formal partition by metes and bounds. The other evidence supported the finding of a prior partition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908, a writing intended to record a formal partition by allotting specific property and declaring exclusive title requires registration. A partition may be oral, and an unregistered writing that does not itself evidence partition by metes and bounds may be used to establish severance of joint status. The Court relied on Nani Bai v. Gita Bai Kom Rama Gunge, Shiromani v. Hem Kumar, Roshan Singh v. Zile Singh, and Sk. Sattar Sk. Mohd. Choudhari v. Gundappa Amabadas Bukate.

predicates.partition_dispute: The parties disputed whether property claimed as joint family property had already been partitioned.
predicates.unregistered_partition_writing: A party relied on a writing about a partition that had not been registered.
predicates.relied_on_to_show_severance: The writing was relied on to show that the family had separated in status, rather than as proof of formal allotments by metes and bounds.

issues.definition: When a partition dispute involves an unregistered writing relied on to show severance, the writing can establish severance but cannot prove formal allotments.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal cannot reverse concurrent decisions on a framed substantial question of law without addressing and setting aside the independent findings that support those decisions.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the partition suit, and the first appellate court affirmed the dismissal after finding a prior partition and considering evidence of the branches’ separate possession and dealings with the properties.
The High Court admitted a second appeal on the question whether the unregistered writing was admissible as a deed of partition.
The High Court reversed the lower courts based on its view that the writing required registration, without addressing or setting aside the first appellate court’s other findings.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court’s judgment did not provide adequate reasons for reversing the lower courts.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in reversing the lower courts without disturbing their other findings; its judgment was set aside and the decisions of the lower courts were restored.
issues.legal_principle: In a regular second appeal, the High Court may interfere with concurrent findings only on a substantial question of law framed or subsequently reframed or substituted. It must address material findings supporting the decisions under appeal and give proper reasons before reversing them. The Court applied Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal from decisions of lower courts.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_findings: The lower courts reached the same result and the appellate court made material findings supporting that result.
predicates.high_court_reverses_without_addressing_m: The High Court reverses the lower courts without addressing or setting aside the material findings supporting their decisions.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when the lower courts have made concurrent decisions supported by material findings, a High Court that reverses without addressing those findings cannot reverse on that basis.
